Home/Blog/Can You Repair Electric Gates Installed by Another Company?
Maintenance

Can You Repair Electric Gates Installed by Another Company?

A different gate company may be able to repair electric gates installed by your original contractor. The answer depends on the equipment, its condition and whether the new engineer can obtain the information and parts needed to work on it. Changing contractors does not, by itself, mean you need new gates. Equally, a company should not promise a repair before it understands the installation.

Start by requesting an assessment of the existing system. Explain who installed it, what has gone wrong and whether anyone has altered it since. Ask the contractor to confirm that it can assess your equipment before you book a visit. You need a clear account of the fault, the proposed work and anything that would prevent the engineer from returning the gates to use.

Explain why you are changing gate companies

You may have bought a property with electric gates, lost contact with the installer or decided to seek another opinion after repeated callouts. Give the new contractor that context without trying to diagnose the fault yourself. A useful opening description might be: the gates opened normally until last week, now one leaf stops short, and the previous invoice records a controller replacement. Use your own observations and documents rather than guesses about which part has failed.

If another contractor has proposed work, send the written findings and quotation. Ask the new engineer to distinguish what they can confirm from what still needs investigation. Avoid reducing the enquiry to whether they can beat the other price: proposals may cover different repairs, inspections or replacement parts. Comparing their scope matters before comparing their totals.

Send useful information before the visit

When arranging electric gate repair and maintenance, provide your postcode and describe whether the entrance has swing gates or a sliding gate. Explain whether the gate is open, closed or stuck partway, and whether you have another way into the property. For a shared entrance, identify the person authorised to arrange work and agree spending.

Gather the records you already hold. Useful material includes the original installation invoice, user instructions, service reports, previous repair invoices and photographs showing the whole entrance. Include the motor and controller model if you can read it from paperwork or an externally accessible label. Do not open an enclosure, reach around a gate or remove a cover to find a serial number.

  • Describe what happened before the fault: a power interruption, building work, vehicle impact, heavy rain or a change to the controls.
  • Say whether the fault is constant or intermittent, and which access method you were using when you noticed it.
  • Identify changes that previous contractors made, even if you do not understand the technical description on the invoice.
  • Provide photographs taken from a safe position, keeping entry codes, passwords and unrelated personal details out of them.

Do not run the gates again simply to create a video for the enquiry. Describe the behaviour you have already seen. The engineer can decide how to investigate it under controlled conditions.

Agree what the first inspection will cover

Ask whether the initial appointment covers fault diagnosis, a wider condition assessment, or both. Request the price and charging basis for that visit, including how the contractor handles additional time or a return appointment. A booking described only as a callout tells you little about the report or work you will receive.

A powered gate combines moving leaves, supports, motors, controls and protective devices. HSE's powered gate safety guidance explains that safety depends on how those parts work together in the particular installation. Ask the engineer to explain any concern about the complete entrance, even if you initially reported only a remote-control or motor problem.

Request written findings that separate the reported fault, any immediate safety concern and optional improvements. If the engineer cannot reach a firm diagnosis during the visit, ask what evidence is missing and what the next investigation would involve. Agree that further chargeable work needs your approval rather than assuming that an inspection authorises an open-ended repair.

Check support for the equipment you already have

Ask about experience with the actual motor and control system, rather than accepting a broad statement about repairing electric gates. Have the contractor identify which parts they expect to retain and which need further checks. If someone proposes a replacement component, request its make and model and an explanation of compatibility with the remaining equipment.

For an older installation, ask the contractor to check current parts support before promising a completion date. If they propose an alternative to the original component, ask why they have chosen it and what associated work it requires. Do not assume a part will fit because its housing looks similar or because the same manufacturer supplied both products.

Where the entrance includes an intercom, keypad or app, include those controls in the discussion. Ask whether the contractor can support the relevant account and programming arrangements or needs another specialist. Transfer administrative access through an agreed private process; do not put gate codes or account passwords into a general quotation email.

Missing paperwork needs a clear plan

Tell the engineer before the visit if the seller or original installer did not leave records. The documents supplied when a completed powered gate first enters service include user instructions and a Declaration of Conformity. Ask what records exist for the assembled installation, as well as manuals for individual components.

If documents are missing, ask the new contractor what they can establish by inspection and what they cannot verify. Request a list of records worth seeking from the previous owner or installer. Do not ask the contractor to treat a component manual as a complete history of the entrance, or assume that a repair visit will reconstruct every detail of the original installation.

Keep warranty questions separate from the repair scope

Before authorising work that might fall under an existing warranty, read the written terms and ask the warranty provider how it wants the fault handled. Ask whether it requires an inspection, authorisation or a particular repair route. Get the answer in writing. The existence of a manufacturer's name on a motor does not tell you what the original installer agreed to cover.

Then ask the new contractor what warranty, if any, it offers on its own proposed work. Separate parts, labour and attendance, and clarify any exclusions for retained equipment. Avoid accepting a verbal promise that leaves you unsure whether a later problem would count as a repeat of the same fault or an unrelated failure.

Compare repair, partial replacement and further investigation

Request an explanation of why the recommended work addresses the fault. If the proposal is to replace the automation, ask whether the engineer has assessed the gates and their supports for continued use. Discuss gate automation kits as a defined option, with a list of what stays and what changes.

Ask for alternatives where the evidence supports them. One proposal might cover a diagnosed component fault; another might replace several linked components. Have the contractor explain what each option resolves, what remains uncertain and what further work it excludes. Do not choose between them using the motor price alone.

If you have already paid for several repairs, bring the reports together and ask whether they describe the same unresolved problem. Use those findings to compare electric gate repair or replacement. A new contractor's opinion should help you make the next decision. It should not rely on dismissing previous work without evidence or on promising that a replacement will never develop another fault.

Agree the condition in which the engineer will leave the gate

The contractor needs to leave the gate in a safe condition and explain the outcome to the user. Ask how the contractor will explain the outcome if repairs cannot finish during the first visit. Request clear instructions on whether the gate may be used, who will arrange the next stage and how residents should manage access meanwhile.

Do not press for continued operation if the engineer identifies an unresolved safety concern. Discuss access needs before the appointment, especially where the driveway is the only vehicle entrance. Follow the installation-specific instructions supplied by the contractor rather than trying a manual-release method from a different gate online.

At handover, request a written description of the work, the fitted parts, the checks completed and any outstanding recommendations. Ask for a demonstration of the controls and the safe shutdown procedure for your installation. Keep those details with your gate records so that the next servicing contractor can see what changed. You can then judge the repair against an agreed scope rather than simply whether the gates moved when the engineer left.

Home/Blog/Electric Gates Open but Won’t Close: Common Causes and Repair Options
Maintenance

Electric Gates Open but Won’t Close: Common Causes and Repair Options

If your electric gates open but will not close, the fault is not necessarily the motor. The controller may be receiving an instruction to keep the entrance open, or a protective input may be preventing closure. A gate that starts closing and then reverses needs a different investigation from one that never attempts to move. The engineer needs to establish which behaviour you are seeing before recommending a repair.

Stop repeated attempts to close the gates and keep people away from their movement area. Note what has already happened, then contact a competent powered-gate contractor. Do not disconnect a sensor, alter the force setting or force a gate leaf into position to secure the entrance. The appropriate repair depends on the installed equipment and the cause of the fault. If the original installer is unavailable, ask about repairing gates installed by another company when booking an assessment.

Describe exactly how the gates fail to close

When booking electric gate repairs, start with the sequence you observed. Say whether the gates reached their normal fully open position, whether both leaves moved and what happened when you expected them to close. Explain whether you normally press a control to close them or whether they close after a waiting period.

Useful distinctions include a gate that stays silent, one that makes a sound without moving, and one that travels before stopping. If it reverses, tell the engineer whether this happened near the same position on previous occasions. Do not repeat the movement to obtain a more precise measurement or to test your theory.

Also describe the practical problem. Are you unable to secure the drive, unable to use the pedestrian route or concerned that the gate could move while someone passes? Include any separate entrance you can use. This helps the contractor discuss arrangements for the visit without assuming that you can safely operate or release the gate yourself.

A safety input may be preventing closure

Photocells and other protective inputs can affect closing differently from opening. The behaviour depends on the controller and its configuration. In the Nice A6/A700F manual (PDF), for example, relevant photocell inputs can prevent closing or cause reversal, and a sustained opening command can keep a gate open. Those are model-specific examples, not a diagnosis of your installation.

From outside the movement area, note anything you can already see around the entrance: a bin in the opening, vegetation near a sensor, a damaged housing or a component knocked out of position. Report the observation. Do not walk into the opening, reach through the gates or reposition a protective device to see whether closure returns.

Ask the engineer whether the controller is receiving a valid safety input and what evidence identifies the fault. If a sensor needs replacement, request an explanation of why replacement is necessary and how the contractor will check its operation with the rest of the system. A repair should resolve the issue without removing the protection that the entrance needs.

The gate may be waiting for a different command

Opening successfully does not establish how the gate is meant to close. Some controllers offer different operating modes. The Nice A5 manual, for example, describes an automatic-close setting and an alternative that waits for another command. Check the user instructions supplied for your own gate; do not copy programming instructions from another model.

Tell the engineer if the behaviour changed after a service, power interruption, control replacement or account change. Ask the people who manage the entrance whether anyone requested a different operating arrangement. On a shared drive, agree who can authorise changes so that a repair does not leave residents with unexpected behaviour.

If remotes, a keypad and an intercom control the same entrance, describe any differences you have already noticed between them. The contractor can investigate the relevant gate access controls alongside the gate itself. Avoid buying another remote simply because the gate has stayed open; first establish whether a replacement remote would address the diagnosed problem.

Stopping or reversing needs a wider assessment

A leaf that starts closing and then stops gives the engineer different information from a gate that never moves. Report scraping, a change in the gap beneath the gate, visible impact damage or unusual movement at a support. For a sliding gate, describe anything you can see on the track from a safe position. These observations are reasons for inspection, not proof that a particular roller, hinge or motor has failed.

HSE's powered gate safety guidance considers the complete installation, including its mountings, environment and response to protective devices. Ask the engineer to explain whether the behaviour follows a control input, resistance during movement or another fault. Do not accept increased closing force as an unexplained substitute for identifying the cause.

If someone proposes work on a hinge, track or gate support, ask how it relates to the symptom and what further checks follow the adjustment. Where the gate operates beside a parked car, wall or pedestrian path, explain how you use that space. Give the contractor the everyday context needed to assess the proposed repair.

Report rain, electrical trips and recent damage

A fault appearing after rain deserves attention, but timing alone does not prove which part is affected. Record whether the behaviour followed wet weather, flooding near the entrance or other work around the gate. If electrical protection has tripped, tell the contractor and avoid repeated attempts to restore operation.

Water ingress and damaged electrical connections can create hazards around powered gates. Keep clear of damaged equipment and leave enclosure inspection and electrical testing to a competent contractor. Do not remove an underground motor cover, open a controller box or attempt to dry internal components yourself.

Ask the engineer to distinguish an affected component from the condition that allowed the problem to develop. If a quotation includes a replacement part, ask whether it also addresses any identified water-entry route, damaged cable protection or support problem. Request a written explanation of any investigation still needed before the contractor can settle the repair scope.

Give the engineer a concise fault record

Prepare a short account before the visit rather than a list of parts you suspect. Include the gate type, equipment details from existing paperwork, the last time it worked normally and any previous repair report. Say whether the current fault repeats an earlier problem and what the contractor changed on that occasion.

  • State the gate's current position and whether a separate entrance remains available.
  • Describe the failed closing sequence using your previous observations.
  • List controls that were in use when the fault occurred, without deliberately cycling the gate again.
  • Record relevant weather, impact, landscaping or electrical work around the time it changed.
  • Attach safe, existing photographs and any fault message visible without opening equipment.

Keep entry codes and passwords out of the record. If the contractor needs administrative access, agree a separate way to provide it. For a managed property, nominate a contact who can explain the entrance's normal operation and approve the next step.

Compare repair options against the diagnosis

The repair proposal should name the identified problem and explain the work needed to address it. Ask whether the price covers investigation only or includes parts, labour, programming and checks after the work. Request clarification of VAT, return visits and any exclusions before authorising the proposal.

Possible recommendations depend on what the engineer finds. Ask whether a proposed sensor replacement addresses a confirmed device fault, whether control work restores the intended operating arrangement, or whether a mechanical repair corrects a problem with gate travel. These are separate decisions; a quotation that says only “make gates close” leaves the scope unclear.

If the engineer recommends replacing several components, ask why repairing the identified fault would not be suitable. Request the alternative scope where one exists, together with its limitations. You do not need an unsupported promise about years of future reliability. You need to understand what the proposed work resolves and which existing parts will remain.

Agree access arrangements and check the handover

If the gates must remain out of use while awaiting parts, ask the contractor to explain the safe arrangement for your entrance. Do not assume manual release will make a damaged or unstable gate safe to move. Follow the instructions supplied for that installation, and tell other residents that its usual operation has changed.

After the repair, request a demonstration of the agreed opening and closing behaviour and an explanation of any changes to controls. Ask for a written record of the diagnosed fault, completed work and outstanding recommendations. Have the engineer explain how to stop operation safely if the problem returns, and keep those instructions with the service records. You should leave the handover knowing what caused the fault, what changed and how to use the repaired installation.

Home/Blog/Electric Gates Keep Breaking Down: Repair Again or Replace the System?
Maintenance

Electric Gates Keep Breaking Down: Repair Again or Replace the System?

Repeated electric-gate breakdowns are a reason to review the whole repair history before approving another callout. Ask whether the failures come from the same unresolved problem, separate worn components or a wider issue with the installation. Then compare a defined repair with partial or complete replacement. The right choice depends on the evidence, the condition of what you would retain and the scope of each proposal.

A gate's age or your frustration with the last breakdown cannot answer that question alone. Nor should a contractor decide it using the price of a new motor without considering the surrounding work. Start with an inspection and a written explanation of the options. You need to know what each option fixes, what it leaves in place and what further spending remains uncertain.

Put the repair history in order

Gather invoices, service reports and any messages explaining previous faults. List when each problem occurred, the symptom you reported, what the contractor diagnosed and what they changed. Include adjustments and programming changes as well as replacement parts. If you cannot find a report, record that gap instead of reconstructing a technical explanation from memory.

Ask the next engineer to compare those records with the current fault. Did the same symptom return after the same repair? Did the earlier contractor complete recommended follow-up work? Did a later change affect equipment that had previously operated as intended? These questions give the assessment a starting point without assuming that every callout had the same cause.

Keep the financial record alongside the technical history, but separate past spending from the decision now in front of you. Money already spent does not tell you whether the next repair addresses the fault. Ask what new evidence supports the present recommendation and whether the contractor has resolved any uncertainty left by the earlier visits.

Ask for a condition assessment, not just another part

When discussing gate repair and maintenance, explain that you need help deciding what to retain. Request findings on the gates, supports, drive equipment and controls, with any limits of the inspection made clear. If you want a fresh assessment, ask about repairing gates installed by another company and provide the earlier records. Ask the contractor to identify the reason behind each recommendation rather than describing the entire installation as old.

Gate safety depends on the assembled system and its circumstances. A replacement motor does not remove the need to consider mounting strength, movement and the interaction of the controls and protective devices. Ask which existing components the proposed work relies on and how the engineer will assess them.

Separate an immediate safety concern from a reliability complaint or an optional improvement. If the engineer considers the gate unsafe, ask for written instructions about taking it out of use and managing access. Do not treat a budget decision about future improvements as permission to keep using equipment that needs safety work first.

When another repair deserves consideration

A further repair deserves a place in the comparison when the contractor can identify a fault, specify an appropriate remedy and explain the condition of the equipment that will remain. Ask why the proposed work should address the current symptom and whether previous repairs dealt with the same issue. Request evidence from the inspection rather than an assurance that this part usually fixes it.

Have the contractor confirm parts availability for the actual model and identify any alternative they propose. Ask what programming, mechanical work or checking accompanies the replacement. If the report identifies an underlying problem, such as damage around the equipment, ask whether the quotation includes addressing it or merely replacing the affected component.

Also ask what would make the contractor reconsider repair once work begins. For example, which currently inaccessible areas still need inspection, and how will you approve additional work if the findings change? This creates a decision point before the bill grows. Avoid agreeing to a succession of substitutions without an explanation of what each investigation has established.

Consider replacing the automation while retaining the gates

Ask whether the assessment supports keeping the gate leaves and supports while replacing the drive equipment and controls. Discuss gate automation kits as a separate proposal. Request an itemised list of retained and replacement components, rather than accepting “new automation” as a complete specification.

Include motors, the control panel, safety devices, remotes, cabling and connections to the intercom in that list. Ask which existing parts the contractor has verified as suitable for the proposed arrangement. If the work changes the gate's movement or control behaviour, request an explanation of what residents will notice and what training they will receive.

HSE's guidance on modifying powered gates explains that significant modifications can require a new conformity assessment. Ask the installer to explain the responsibilities and documentation applicable to the proposed work. Do not assume that replacing an individual component and creating a substantially changed powered-gate system carry identical requirements.

Give complete replacement a defined scope

If a contractor recommends new gates as well as new automation, ask what findings justify that extent of work. Request an explanation of why retaining the present leaves, hinges or supports would be unsuitable. Where the recommendation also changes the gate type, ask for a drawing that shows the proposed movement, parking position and route for people on foot.

A quotation for a complete automated gate system needs to identify more than the visible gates and motors. Ask about removal, foundations, electrical work, drainage, access controls and making good the driveway. Have the installer state which existing services or structures it intends to reuse and what remains subject to the site survey.

Include planning checks in the allocation of responsibilities where the design or boundary would change. Do not assume that describing work as replacement settles the permissions question. Ask who will check the relevant property constraints before you order, without relying on a general statement that all replacement gates follow the same rule.

Compare totals that cover the same outcome

Set the proposals beside each other and mark what each includes. A fault repair, an automation replacement and a new entrance deliver different scopes, so the lowest headline figure does not establish the best choice. Ask each contractor to describe the completed result in plain language and to identify exclusions.

  • Investigation and preparation: inspection, further testing, removal and disposal, and work needed before installation can begin.
  • Equipment and building work: the named components, gate supports, cable routes, drainage and reinstatement included in that proposal.
  • Completion: programming, checks, instructions, documentation and demonstration of the controls.
  • Commercial terms: whether VAT applies and is included, payment stages, variation approval and written warranty conditions.

Ask about retained parts explicitly. If a repair keeps the existing intercom and cabling, record that. If a replacement quote also keeps them, do not assume it provides a completely new system throughout. Make the contractors resolve differences in scope before you compare their totals.

Include disruption and access in the decision

Explain how a gate outage affects your household or property. You may need a clear pedestrian route, space for visitors to wait or arrangements for residents who arrive at different times. Ask each contractor how it proposes to manage access during the work and what you must arrange beforehand.

For a shared entrance, identify who can approve the expenditure and who communicates with users. Ask how the contractor will hand over remotes, account administration and changed entry arrangements. Keep security credentials separate from general notices. A technically suitable proposal still needs a workable plan for the people who use the entrance.

Request a programme based on confirmed equipment availability and the assessed work. Do not assume that another contractor's suggested duration applies to your installation. If access arrangements depend on a particular date, explain that constraint before accepting the quotation and ask how delays would be handled.

Ask what support follows the work

Request written warranty terms for each option and distinguish parts cover from labour or attendance. Ask how the contractor handles a recurring fault and what it excludes where existing equipment remains. Do not fill gaps in one proposal using promises made by another company or a general claim about the manufacturer's reputation.

Ask for the maintenance and inspection recommendations relevant to the completed installation. Powered gates need regular checks and maintenance. Have the contractor explain the tasks for a competent engineer and any routine care that the user instructions allow you to undertake. Record the proposed servicing scope instead of assuming every service visit includes the same work.

Make the decision from the findings

Before accepting another repair, ask yourself whether you can explain the diagnosis and why the proposed work addresses it. Before accepting replacement, ask whether you understand what will remain, what will change and why. If either answer is unclear, request clarification in the written proposal before committing.

Then agree the acceptance and handover arrangements. Request the work record, relevant instructions and an account of any outstanding limitations. Ask the contractor to demonstrate the agreed operation and explain the response to a future fault. Keep the new documents with the previous reports so that the next decision starts with evidence. That gives you a practical basis for choosing a repair, an automation upgrade or a replacement entrance.

Home/Blog/Can You Replace Gate Automation Without Replacing the Gates?
Maintenance

Can You Replace Gate Automation Without Replacing the Gates?

Yes, you may be able to replace the automation while keeping your existing driveway gates. A competent installer needs to assess the gate leaves, supports and movement, then specify equipment that works with the parts you retain. Keeping the gates does not mean keeping every motor, cable or control, and an attractive entrance can still need mechanical repairs before new automation goes in.

This option suits a different question from whether to approve another fault repair. You have decided to investigate new drive equipment and now need to understand the work around it. For an earlier comparison of the options, read about repairing or replacing gates that keep breaking down. Here, the focus is what an automation replacement should include when you want the visible gates to stay.

Separate the gates from the equipment you want to change

Start by describing what you want to preserve: the appearance of the entrance, the gate leaves, the brick piers, or all of those. Then describe what you want the replacement to do. You might want to replace unsupported equipment, address a diagnosed recurring problem or change how residents operate the entrance. Give the contractor the reason for the project before discussing a particular motor.

Ask for a retained-and-replaced list. It should name the gates and supports, motors, brackets, control panel, protective devices, power supply, cables, remotes and entry controls. Mark anything the installer has not yet inspected as provisional. That list gives you a useful way to compare quotations and avoids discovering halfway through the work that you and the contractor understood “new automation” differently.

Check the structure and movement before choosing motors

The installer needs to assess how the gates move and what carries their weight. For swing gates, discuss the leaves, hinges, mounting points and supports. For sliding gates, the assessment should cover the support and guidance arrangement along the travel path. Describe scraping, sagging or changes in alignment, even if the old automation could still move the gate.

HSE treats powered-gate safety as a question about the assembled installation and its surroundings. Stronger drive equipment is not a substitute for resolving a defective structure or unsuitable movement. Ask the engineer to separate mechanical repairs from the automation specification so you can see what makes retaining the gates viable. Have them explain any recommendation to change the supports or the gate design.

Leave manual movement checks and release procedures to someone who understands the installation. A gate that looks manageable can move unexpectedly once its drive no longer restrains it. You can help by collecting records and describing symptoms without opening control enclosures or disconnecting equipment.

Specify a replacement for this entrance

An installer should select the drive arrangement for the actual gate and its use. The existing motor's brand or outward appearance cannot establish that another model will fit. Provide any readable model details from accessible labels, together with earlier installation drawings. The contractor should verify the relevant equipment information rather than build a quotation around a photograph alone.

Discuss where new equipment would sit. On a swing gate, ask whether the proposed brackets and operator position require changes to the leaf or pier. If you have underground operators, ask whether the proposal retains their housings and how the installer will assess those areas. For a sliding gate, ask what the replacement involves at the drive and its connection to the gate. Request a sketch if the explanation is hard to picture.

When comparing automation for existing driveway gates, have the contractor identify the proposed equipment and the parts it relies on. Do not treat a boxed kit's component list as the complete specification for your entrance. Include any additional work in the written proposal before you place the order.

Decide what happens to cables, remotes and the intercom

Keeping the gates does not establish whether the old electrical supply and cabling can stay. Ask the contractor to inspect the existing provision, explain what it can reuse and identify any areas it cannot assess without further access. Cable routes beneath a finished driveway deserve attention at the survey stage, particularly if avoiding disturbance is a priority for you.

Tell the installer how you operate the entrance now. List remotes, keypads, intercoms, phone access and any arrangements for visitors. Discuss gate access controls alongside the replacement controller. A working intercom still needs a compatibility check with the proposed system; the installer should confirm which functions will remain available.

For a shared entrance, appoint someone to coordinate the change. Keep a record of how many authorised users need access, who holds programming information and who can manage any connected account. Agree how the contractor will issue replacement controls or transfer access. Share credentials through an appropriate private channel, rather than putting them in a notice circulated to every resident.

Include a fresh review of protective measures

Changing the automation affects the equipment that controls gate movement. The installer needs to consider the complete arrangement, including the retained parts, protective devices and the way people use the entrance. Existing photocells alone do not demonstrate that a replacement system will be safe. Ask how the assessment addresses the gate's movement and the places where someone could become trapped.

HSE's guidance on modifying powered gates explains that significant modifications can require a new conformity assessment. Ask the installer to explain how that applies to the proposed scope and who will take responsibility for the completed installation. A component repair and a substantial alteration do not necessarily have the same implications.

Request the relevant assessment, checks and handover documents as part of the quotation. Ask the contractor to identify any restriction on using the existing gates before the work starts. If an engineer has advised taking the system out of use, agree safe temporary access instead of continuing to operate it while you compare prices.

Compare the whole installation price

A motor price leaves too much unanswered for this decision. Obtain an itemised installed quotation that describes both the new equipment and the work needed around it. You can then compare the contractor's proposal with another offer without assuming they include the same retained components or preparation.

  • Preparation: assessment, removal of redundant equipment, repairs to retained gates or supports, and disposal.
  • Installation: named drive equipment and controls, protective measures, electrical work, cable routes and any drainage work identified at the survey.
  • Finishing: repairs to paving or finishes, programming, checks, user instructions and a demonstration.
  • Terms: whether VAT applies and is included, payment stages, exclusions, warranty conditions and approval of extra work.

Keeping sound gates may avoid replacing those leaves, but it does not establish a fixed saving on the overall project. Additional structural or electrical work can change the comparison. Ask each contractor to identify uncertain items and explain when it will be able to price them. Agree an approval point for extra work before anyone removes equipment or opens up the driveway.

Plan access while the work takes place

Explain how you need to use the entrance during the project. Include pedestrian access, vehicle movements and deliveries that you cannot rearrange. Ask who will secure the site when work stops for the day and what you should do if the gates cannot return to use as expected. Agree a programme based on the surveyed work and confirmed equipment availability.

A different contractor may be able to undertake the replacement. If your original installer is unavailable, read about working on gates installed by another company, and supply the new engineer with the records you have. Confirm acceptance of the existing installation before assuming another firm can support every retained component.

Check the handover against the quotation

Before the contractor finishes, work through the retained-and-replaced list together. Ask them to record any changes agreed during installation and show you how to operate the finished system. Arrange for the person who manages a shared entrance to attend, so that operating instructions reach the people who need them.

  1. Check that the work record identifies the fitted equipment and the existing parts that remain.
  2. Request the relevant instructions and assessment or testing records for the completed work.
  3. Ask for a demonstration of normal operation and the approved arrangements for a power failure or fault.
  4. Confirm maintenance recommendations, support contacts and the written warranty terms, including treatment of retained equipment.

Keep these documents with the previous service history. HSE advises that powered gates need maintenance to remain safe; your installer should explain the arrangements for this particular installation. You should leave the handover knowing what changed, what stayed, how to use the entrance and who to contact if it behaves differently. That is the practical test of a replacement proposal that keeps the gates you want to retain.

Home/Blog/Electric Gate Remote Not Working? Remote, Receiver or Gate Fault?
Maintenance

Electric Gate Remote Not Working? Remote, Receiver or Gate Fault?

An electric gate remote that stops working does not, by itself, show that the gate motor has failed. The fault could involve the handset, its battery, the radio receiver or the wider gate system. The most useful starting point is what you have already noticed: does a second authorised remote still work, and do the usual keypad or intercom controls behave differently?

A light on the remote is not confirmation that the gate has accepted the command. Equally, an entrance that stays shut is not a reason to order a replacement motor. Describe the symptoms first, then have the relevant equipment checked before buying parts. This guide explains how to prepare for that conversation without opening electrical enclosures or altering the gate's safety settings.

Start with the gate's condition, not repeated button presses

Before trying another control, look from a safe position outside the gate's movement area. If the gate is damaged, hanging unevenly, moving unpredictably or presenting a trapping risk, stop using it and arrange competent assistance. Keep people away from the hazard. Do not repeatedly command a gate that has already behaved dangerously just to see whether the remote works this time.

The HSE's powered-gate safety basics explain the need to keep these systems safe and take dangerous equipment out of use. Follow the installation's documented emergency arrangements where it is safe to do so. Do not improvise a manual release, bridge a safety input or reach into a motor housing. If you cannot access the property safely, explain that when requesting help so temporary access can be discussed.

What happens between pressing the remote and the gate moving?

For a radio-controlled installation, the handset sends a command that a compatible receiver must recognise. The gate controller then has to act on the relevant input, within the installation's operating and protective arrangements. That creates several places for an investigation to start; the remote is only one part of the process.

Ask the contractor to distinguish three questions: is the handset transmitting the intended command, is the receiver recognising it, and is the gate controller able to carry it out? Those questions help define the investigation. They do not require you to open the control box or check live terminals. A handset indicator alone cannot answer all three, and different installations can use different receiver and controller arrangements.

One remote has failed, but another still works

If a second authorised handset has recently operated the gate normally, mention that first. It gives the engineer a useful comparison and makes an individual handset or its enrolment worth investigating. It does not prove which component is faulty, particularly if the problem is intermittent or the two observations were made under different conditions.

Check the failed remote's identification against its instructions. A battery replacement may be an appropriate user task where the manufacturer provides a procedure. Use the specified battery and polarity; do not substitute a different type because it fits. If the case is damaged, has been wet or will not open as described, stop and ask the supplier or installer rather than forcing it apart.

For one specific example, Nice's Era Flor instructions describe reduced range and a delayed or dim indicator as possible signs of an exhausted battery. These are model-specific observations, not a universal fault code for every remote. The correct manual matters more than a generic online button sequence.

All the remotes have stopped working

Several handsets failing around the same time warrants a different discussion from one damaged fob. Tell the contractor whether the usual keypad, intercom release or another authorised control has continued to work. Use observations from normal, safe operation; there is no need to repeatedly cycle the entrance or involve neighbours in an improvised test.

If another control still operates the gate, the radio command path is a reasonable area for the engineer to investigate. That is a diagnostic lead, not proof that a new receiver is required. If none of the normal controls works, the investigation needs to cover the installation more broadly. Note any known power interruption, recent work or change in behaviour, without opening electrical equipment to look for a cause.

Where the gate responds by opening but then stays open, the symptom needs a different assessment. Our guide to electric gates that open but will not close covers that distinction. A working opening command does not establish why the closing movement is unavailable.

The remote works only close to the gate

Reduced range is useful information, especially if it is a recent change. Record where you normally use the remote and whether the behaviour varies by time or handset. Compare like with like where ordinary use allows: a report that one fob works from the drive while another fails from inside a vehicle needs that context attached.

Battery condition and radio interference are among the possibilities described in manufacturer guidance, but distance alone is not a diagnosis. Avoid buying a range extender or moving an aerial on that evidence. Give the engineer the observations and ask whether the transmitter, receiver installation and local radio conditions need checking. Do not walk into the gate's swing or travel area to find the closest point at which it responds.

A matching-looking replacement may be the wrong remote

Before ordering a replacement, establish the handset model and the receiver it must work with. Appearance is not enough. Manufacturer instructions specify compatible coding systems and receiver arrangements; the Nice example above also directs users to the relevant receiver or controller instructions for memorisation. A product described simply as a gate remote is not a compatibility assessment.

Provide photographs of accessible handset labels and any existing installation paperwork. Let the engineer identify equipment inside electrical enclosures. Ask the supplier to confirm compatibility and explain what programming or enrolment is included in the price. If the original model is unavailable, request an explanation of the proposed replacement route before agreeing to change other equipment.

For a shared entrance, the managing agent or person responsible for access should authorise new handsets. Avoid following a generic reset procedure: it may change settings or remove access that other residents depend on. If a remote is lost, ask whether that particular system can remove its access and what the consequences would be for the remaining users. Do not assume every receiver supports the same management functions.

A button works differently, or only one gate leaf opens

Different buttons may be assigned different functions. For example, the manufacturer's programming arrangements may allow a button to be associated with a chosen controller command. An unexpected response therefore needs to be compared with the intended setup, rather than immediately attributed to a failed motor.

Explain which button you used, what normally happens and what happened this time. If only one leaf moves, record whether this is the usual pedestrian-access function or a new symptom. The engineer can check the command assignment and the installation's behaviour together. Do not alter programming merely to make both leaves move, and do not assume an intercom that rings successfully has also delivered a valid opening command.

What to tell the repair contractor

A short factual description is more useful than a list of parts you think need replacing. For help with the entrance's remotes, keypads and access controls, prepare the information available without dismantling anything:

  • The handset brand and model, where readable, plus any installation or maintenance paperwork.
  • Whether one remote or every remote is affected, and what other controls have done during normal use.
  • Whether there is no response, delayed response, reduced range or an unexpected movement.
  • When the issue began, whether it is intermittent, and any known damage, power interruption or recent work.
  • Whether the entrance serves one home or several, and who can authorise access changes.

If the original installer is unavailable, say so when booking. Read about having gates repaired by another company for the records and access arrangements that can help a new contractor assess the installation. Keep remote programming details and access codes private; provide them only through an agreed secure process if they are needed.

Agree the repair scope and check the handover

Ask for the diagnostic work to be distinguished from any proposed replacement. A quotation should make clear whether it covers a handset, enrolment, receiver work or investigation of a wider gate fault. Confirm how additional work will be approved. A remote problem alone is not a sufficient explanation for replacing the whole automation system; the contractor should identify the fault and justify the recommended scope.

Before the job is closed, use this practical handover checklist with the responsible contractor:

  1. Confirm which fault was found and which equipment or settings changed.
  2. Confirm the intended function of each supplied button and any retained access controls.
  3. Agree how authorised users will receive their remotes and operating instructions.
  4. Record the equipment details, future battery guidance and who to contact if the symptom returns.

The aim is a working entrance with understood controls and a documented repair. Keep the explanation, invoice and updated instructions together so the next person maintaining the gates can see what was changed.

Home/Blog/Gate Intercom Rings but Won’t Open the Gate | Repair or Replace?
Maintenance

Gate Intercom Rings but Won’t Open the Gate | Repair or Replace?

If your gate intercom rings and you can speak to a visitor, but the gate stays closed when you press the release button, the fault needs tracing beyond the call itself. You may have a problem with the release command, the intercom's output, the connection to the gate controller or the gate installation. A successful conversation does not prove that the opening command reached its destination.

You do not necessarily need a new intercom or new gate motors. Start with a clear account of what still works, which users have the problem and what changed before it began. An engineer can use that information to narrow the investigation and explain whether a repair, configuration change or replacement makes sense.

Keep people clear before investigating

Do not keep pressing release while somebody pushes or pulls the gate. Keep visitors, children and vehicles outside its movement area. If the gate moves unpredictably, has visible damage or presents an electrical hazard, stop using it and contact a competent contractor. Follow the documented safe shutdown arrangements for your installation if you can do so without approaching danger.

The HSE's powered-gate safety guidance explains why dangerous gates should remain out of use until the safety concerns have been addressed. Do not bridge terminals, remove covers or bypass a safety device to see whether the gate will move. Use another safe entrance if one is available. Tell the contractor if you cannot enter or leave the property through your normal route.

Describe exactly what happens during the call

Separate the sequence into observations. Does the visitor's button ring the indoor handset, your mobile or both? Can each person hear the other? Does the screen show the expected entrance? What happens after you use the normal release control? Record an error message or unfamiliar symbol without assuming what it means.

Give the engineer a short description such as: the front-gate call reaches both residents, audio works, but neither resident can open the vehicle gate from the call. That provides more useful information than saying the whole intercom is dead. If the pedestrian entrance still releases, name it separately so the engineer knows there are different entrances or outputs to investigate.

  • Identify the intercom make and model from your paperwork or an accessible external label.
  • Note whether all residents are affected or only one phone, handset or app account.
  • Record when the fault started and whether it followed a phone change, router replacement, service visit or power interruption.
  • Describe what the other authorised controls did during recent normal use, without repeatedly operating a suspect gate for a test.

The remote works but the intercom does not

If your usual remote opened the gate during normal use but the intercom release did not, tell the contractor. That comparison can help focus the first checks on the intercom's command route. It does not certify the gate as safe or rule out an intermittent fault elsewhere.

If you have a remote that also fails to open the gate, include that detail before booking an intercom replacement. Ask the contractor to assess both symptoms together. You want to avoid paying for a new entrance panel only to discover that the gate still refuses commands from several controls.

Keep the timing precise. A remote that worked last month provides different evidence from one that worked just before the intercom failed today. Note whether the entrance has behaved consistently since then, and leave controlled fault testing to the engineer if there is any concern about its movement.

A mobile call connects but the release key does nothing

Telephone-based intercoms may use keypad tones, known as DTMF, to recognise a release instruction during a call. Commtel's intercom fault-finding advice describes cases where users can answer but cannot open the entrance because the equipment does not recognise those tones. Its guidance identifies Wi-Fi Calling and network conditions as possible factors for its systems. This is a product-specific investigation route, not proof that your mobile network caused the fault.

Tell the engineer which phone receives the call and whether the problem started after changing the phone, provider or calling settings. Follow the user instructions for your own intercom; do not copy release keys or programming sequences from a different model. An authorised administrator or manufacturer support team can confirm the correct procedure before anyone changes the stored settings.

A video picture appears but the app will not open the gate

Treat the picture, the on-screen command and the physical gate response as separate observations. Ask the administrator to confirm that your account has access to the intended entrance and that the release control addresses the correct output. This matters particularly where one system serves a vehicle gate and a pedestrian door.

For example, 2N's switch configuration documentation describes configurable outputs, activation methods and switch behaviour. The available options depend on the device and setup. Do not assume that a similar-looking button in another manufacturer's app performs the same function, or change output timing to compensate for an unexplained failure.

Send the contractor a screenshot of the error or button state if it helps, with names, access codes and account details removed. Keep passwords private. If an installer needs access to administer the system, agree an authorised method and who will control the account after the work.

A click or confirmation does not identify the failed part

An engineer needs to establish what the intercom actually switched and whether the connected equipment received the expected instruction. A relay is a switching component; hearing a click does not establish the condition of everything connected after it. Describe the sound if you already noticed it, but do not stand beside moving hardware to listen for it.

Manufacturer equipment also offers different output arrangements. Aiphone's RY-IP44 network adaptor has configurable contact outputs that can respond to door release or call activity. That example shows why the engineer must identify the installed hardware and its configuration before interpreting a response. It is not a recommendation to add that adaptor to an unrelated system.

Ask for a diagnosis that distinguishes the entrance panel, any interface or lock equipment, the cable connection and the gate controller. Where the investigation identifies a wider gate fault, the quotation should explain that scope rather than describe all work as an intercom repair.

Decide whether to repair or replace the intercom

Repair is worth considering when the contractor can identify the fault and support the proposed fix. Ask which part or setting needs attention, how the diagnosis was reached and what evidence will confirm that the work resolved your particular symptom. A quotation for a replacement panel should say why the existing panel cannot sensibly be retained.

Replacement may be worth comparing if suitable parts are unavailable, the existing equipment no longer supports the access arrangements you need, or the contractor cannot offer a dependable repair. Ask for those limitations in writing. Age alone gives you little basis for choosing between an isolated repair and a complete system change.

Keep the scope clear. Replacing the intercom does not automatically mean replacing the driveway gates, motors, indoor monitors and every cable. Equally, you should not assume those components will work with a new panel. Ask the installer to list what can remain, what needs replacement and what still requires inspection. Our guide to choosing a gate intercom covers the broader purchasing decision if replacement becomes the preferred option.

Compare quotations against the same fault and access needs

Request an itemised proposal so you can see what each contractor has allowed for. A lower total may exclude cable investigation, indoor equipment or account setup that another quote includes. Avoid choosing solely on the appearance of the outdoor panel when your main problem is unreliable release.

  1. Ask the contractor to record the reported symptom and the findings from inspection.
  2. Request separate descriptions of repair work, replacement equipment and optional upgrades.
  3. Confirm which existing controls and entrances the completed system will support.
  4. Ask about any ongoing service, connectivity or account charges before accepting a proposal.
  5. Agree the completion checks, documentation and arrangements for reporting a recurring fault.

For a shared London driveway, appoint one person to coordinate residents' reports and authorise changes. Provide a list of required access arrangements without circulating residents' private telephone numbers more widely than necessary. Agree how visitors will reach residents during the work and who will approve changes to communal equipment.

Check the handover before considering the job complete

Ask the engineer to demonstrate the repaired release function using the normal controls and each relevant entrance under safe conditions. If the original fault affected one particular resident, include that person's authorised device in the agreed checks. A successful demonstration from the installer's phone alone may leave your original complaint unresolved.

Get a written explanation of the work, any settings changed and any limitations that remain. Keep the user instructions and responsible contractor's details with your gate records. Ask who administers residents' access and how to request a change when somebody moves out or replaces a phone.

When arranging gate repair and maintenance, send your postcode, intercom details and a brief description of the failed release. Include what other controls still do, who experiences the fault and any recent changes. That gives the contractor a useful starting point for investigating the problem and quoting for the work your entrance needs.

Home/Blog/Why Does Only One Electric Gate Open?
Maintenance

Why Does Only One Electric Gate Open?

If only one leaf of your electric driveway gates opens, the cause may be an intended pedestrian-opening command, a delay between the leaves, or a fault affecting one side. The useful starting point is whether the same control used to open both leaves and whether the stationary leaf moves at all.

One moving leaf does not prove that the other motor needs replacing. This guide covers paired swing gates: two leaves, each hinged to its own outer support. Tell the engineer if you have a different arrangement, such as linked telescopic sliding panels, because the drive layout and investigation will differ.

Check whether you selected pedestrian opening

Look at your handover instructions or the labels on your normal controls. Some installations provide a separate command for walking access. A different remote button, keypad command or intercom release may therefore produce a different opening from the vehicle-access control. Establish which function you requested before reporting a failed motor.

For a specific example, Nice’s MC424L instructions describe one partial-opening option that opens a single leaf, and another that opens both leaves partway. The selected function depends on the installation’s programming. This explains how one leaf can open by design; it does not identify the settings on your gates.

Write down the button you used and what it previously did. If the behaviour changed after someone supplied a replacement remote or altered access settings, include that history. Ask the installer to confirm the intended full-opening command. Avoid guessing programming sequences from a video or resetting the controller to see what happens.

Distinguish a normal delay from a leaf that never starts

Paired leaves need not begin moving together. The MC424L manual, for example, provides a leaf-delay setting. Your installer should explain the sequence for your own entrance, particularly where the leaves meet or overlap. A familiar staggered start is different from a new failure to complete the opening.

Describe the full event you observed during normal use. Did the second leaf start later, make a small movement, stop at the same point, or remain still throughout? Say whether this happened once or on several separate occasions. An account of the complete sequence gives the engineer more to work with than “one side is slow”.

Do not keep cycling a suspect gate to collect a better example. If you already have a recording from a fixed camera, you can share the relevant clip privately with the contractor. Remove unrelated footage and access details. There is no need to stand in the entrance to film another attempt.

Stop using the entrance if the movement looks unsafe

Keep people and vehicles clear if a leaf jerks, leans, scrapes heavily or moves unexpectedly. Stop pressing the controls. Follow the safe shutdown arrangements in your user instructions only if you can reach them without entering a hazardous area. A moving leaf can still create a trapping risk while its partner remains stationary.

The HSE’s powered-gate safety guidance says dangerous gates should remain out of use until the safety concerns have been addressed. Do not push a powered leaf, bridge safety inputs or open electrical covers. Arrange competent help if you cannot establish a safe way to use or secure the entrance.

Compare what the existing controls have done

Tell the contractor whether the problem affects your remote, the intercom release and any other authorised control. Use observations you already have from safe, normal operation. If the vehicle-opening button on one handset operated both leaves while another button opened one, the contractor can investigate their assigned functions. If the same leaf stayed still whichever control you used, say so.

Record the time of each observation. A handset that worked six months ago offers a weaker comparison than one that worked before the fault appeared that morning. Also explain whether a visitor or resident used a different access method. On a shared entrance, ask one nominated person to collect these reports so the engineer receives a consistent account.

Our guide to remote-control problems explains the distinction between the handset, receiver and command reaching the controller. Keep this single-leaf report focused on which side moves and which opening you expected. There is little value in buying another remote before the contractor has checked whether the original command is correct.

What the engineer may investigate on the stationary side

An engineer needs to trace the installed system rather than diagnose it from the appearance of the gate. They can assess the gate’s physical movement, its drive equipment, the relevant controls and the condition of the connections. Ask them to explain which finding accounts for the difference between the two leaves.

The Benincà BRAINY control-unit specification illustrates why the two sides need separate consideration: it supports one or two actuators, with separate motor limit-switch inputs and adjustments. It also distinguishes pedestrian, opening and safety inputs. These features are specific to that controller; another installation may use different equipment and diagnostics.

  • Gate and supports: report visible leaning, a changed gap, scraping marks or damage after an impact. Leave movement checks and any dismantling to the contractor.
  • Drive and release mechanism: mention any recent manual operation, servicing or work around the motor. Describe what happened without assuming that the motor has burnt out.
  • Command and control: ask whether the intended opening instruction reaches the controller and whether its configuration matches the installed pair of gates.
  • Position and protective devices: ask the engineer to interpret the installed system’s indications and verify its response. A light or a click alone does not establish a safe repair.

If the contractor proposes a replacement component, ask what inspection or measurement supports that recommendation. A clear explanation should connect the reported symptom with the finding and the proposed work. You should also know whether the quotation includes checking the completed pair of gates or only fitting a part.

If it started after a power cut or manual release

Tell the engineer who released the gates, which leaf they moved and whether they followed the instructions for that operator. Ask them to check the release and re-engagement arrangements if you are uncertain. Do not force a release lever or copy instructions intended for a different motor. Our manual gate-release guide explains the precautions and paperwork to check.

Separate events in your report: the power went off, someone moved one leaf, power returned, and then you noticed the symptom. That sequence helps the engineer choose their checks. It does not prove that the power cut erased the settings, damaged a board or caused the motor to fail. Avoid a factory reset while the cause remains unclear.

If one leaf starts moving and then stops

A leaf that starts moving and then stops presents a different symptom from one that never responds. Note where it stopped, whether it reversed and whether you noticed contact with the ground or another object. Report recent paving, landscaping or damage near the entrance. Do not move into its travel area to check clearance while the system can operate.

Do not increase the force setting to overcome the symptom. The contractor should assess the complete installation and the safety measures relevant to it. Ask for an explanation of any adjustment and the checks completed afterwards. The fact that both leaves move again does not, by itself, show that the original fault or safety concern has been resolved.

Can you keep using just the working leaf?

Ask the responsible contractor to confirm an arrangement for your particular entrance. An installation with a documented pedestrian-opening function differs from a faulty pair that happens to leave a narrow gap. Consider how residents would enter and leave, where vehicles would wait, and how you would secure the stationary leaf. Do not treat a convenient opening as permission to continue using a suspect system.

Manufacturers also define partial opening differently. FAAC’s E124 product information describes a programmable pedestrian-opening percentage. The presence of such a feature on one controller does not establish the opening width, permitted use or safe settings for yours. Obtain the instructions and a demonstration for the actual installation.

Prepare a useful repair enquiry

Send a short account of the fault with your postcode and any accessible make or model information. Describe the affected leaf from a fixed viewpoint, for example “the right-hand leaf when looking in from the street”. Left and right alone can confuse a conversation when the resident and engineer picture opposite sides of the entrance.

  1. State which leaf opens, which stays still, and whether either leaf starts then stops or reverses.
  2. Name the control used and whether that exact command previously opened both leaves.
  3. Give the date the problem began and mention a power cut, manual release, impact or recent work.
  4. Explain whether the entrance serves one household or several, and describe any urgent access difficulty.
  5. Ask about the inspection charge, approval for additional work and what the engineer will provide after the repair.

Keep photographs limited to views you can take from a safe position. An overall entrance view and an externally readable product label may help the contractor prepare. You do not need to remove covers or expose wiring. If another company fitted the gates, send whatever handover and service records you hold rather than delaying the enquiry because you lack the original invoice.

Agree the repair scope and handover

Request an itemised proposal that distinguishes investigation, repair parts and optional replacement work. Ask which existing equipment can remain and why any wider change is necessary. A fault affecting one leaf does not automatically justify replacing both motors or the complete gate installation. If the engineer recommends a matched replacement, ask them to explain the compatibility or support limitation.

Before accepting the handover, ask the contractor to demonstrate the agreed vehicle and pedestrian functions under safe conditions, explain any changed controls and provide the relevant records. Keep the repaired entrance’s instructions with the responsible contractor’s details. For electric gate repair and maintenance, your enquiry should make the single-leaf symptom clear so the discussion starts with the problem you need resolved.
